Mesopotamia.q: A historian says Avraham's story begins in a wealthy, river-watered region. Which detail from your evidence packet best supports this?
Mesopotamia.right: Canals from two rivers irrigated its fields
wrong: Its farms depended on seasonal rainfall alone
It had no cities, only nomads and herders in tents
Ur was part of a highly developed urban civilization.
It was a small coastal strip on the Mediterranean Sea
Mesopotamia.exp: The Tigris and Euphrates supported irrigation, grain and wealth.

Mesopotamia.q: Why does the evidence packet make leaving Mesopotamia look like a real sacrifice?
Mesopotamia.right: It was a rich, river-watered land
wrong: It was a dry desert where farming depended only on uncertain seasonal rain
It was already Avraham's promised land
He was told to leave it.
Mesopotamia.exp: The Tigris and Euphrates made Mesopotamia part of the wealthy Fertile Crescent.

Ur.q: Which detail would a wealthy household in Ur most likely give as a reason to stay?
Ur.right: Settled wealth, trade and family networks
wrong: Canaan was empty land that nobody had claimed yet
The packet says Canaan was already inhabited; that is not a reason to stay anyway.
Ur depended on rainfall that failed in some years
Ur relied on river irrigation; Canaan relied on rainfall.
Ur had no temples, writing or organized government
Ur had temples, writing and officials.
Ur.exp: Ur offered an established life: livestock, goods, land rights and family and business ties.

Ur.q: Which comparison between Ur and Canaan is supported by the evidence packet?
Ur.right: Ur had irrigation; Canaan relied on rain
wrong: Canaan had larger cities, more temples and more writing than the city of Ur
Ur had the canals, temples and writing.
Canaan was inhabited; Ur was a city.
Ur.exp: Ur used irrigation canals; Canaan was farmed with rain.

Canaan.q: According to the evidence packet, which risk did a household moving to Canaan face that Ur's farmers faced less?
wrong: Floods from the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
Those rivers are in Mesopotamia, not Canaan.
Having no neighbors or other peoples nearby
Canaan was already inhabited by different groups.
A total lack of trade routes in or out of the region
Routes linked Canaan to Egypt, the north and the coast.
Canaan.exp: Canaan depended on rainfall, so drought and famine were serious dangers.

Canaan.q: A student says Avraham went to an empty land. Which evidence best challenges this?
wrong: Canaan had irrigation canals and temples just like the great city of Ur
That's Ur, and it doesn't address the claim.
Location doesn't show it was inhabited.
Canaan.exp: The evidence packet says Canaan was already inhabited.

Haran.q: On the trade-route map, which city sits between Ur and Canaan?
wrong: Babylon is in southern Mesopotamia near Ur, not between Ur and Canaan.
Egypt is beyond Canaan, not between Ur and Canaan.
Goshen is the region in Egypt where Jacob's family settled.
Haran.exp: The route ran Ur → Haran → Canaan → Egypt.

Haran.q: Why does Haran matter in Avraham's story?
Haran.right: He was living there when G-d called him
wrong: It was the city in Canaan where Avraham finally settled at the end of his journey
It was where he was born
Avraham was born in Mesopotamia; the card places the call in Haran.
It was where the Akeida happened
Haran.exp: Haran, on the route between Ur and Canaan, is where Avraham was living at the call.

Dangers of travel.q: Why does the evidence packet's description of travel make Avraham's departure more striking?
Dangers of travel.right: It shows how costly and risky leaving was
wrong: It proves Avraham traveled by sea to Canaan
It shows travel was quick and completely safe
It lists many dangers and long travel times.
It explains why Avraham never reached Canaan
Dangers of travel.exp: Leaving meant risking a long, dangerous journey.

Dangers of travel.q: Which conclusion about Avraham's departure is best supported by the travel evidence?
Dangers of travel.right: Going meant real risk to his household
wrong: The trip was short and safe, so leaving cost Avraham almost nothing at all
Trips took weeks or months with many dangers.
Dangers of travel.exp: Weeks or months, with weather, terrain, thirst, illness, theft and attack.

Lech lecha.q: Which detail of Genesis 12:1 shows that Avraham did not know where he was going?
Lech lecha.right: "to the land that I will show you"
wrong: "I will make of you a great nation"
That is a promise, not a statement about the destination.
That names a companion, not the destination.
"Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?"
That is from the Sodom story in Genesis 18.
Lech lecha.exp: The destination is not named; G-d will show it.

Lech lecha.q: What makes lech lecha a test of trust?
Lech lecha.right: Avraham must go without knowing where
wrong: Avraham is told the exact route and the name of the land before he leaves
G-d says 'the land I will show you.'
Avraham must build an altar first
Lech lecha.exp: 'To the land I will show you': he isn't told the destination.

Three things left behind.q: Why might the Torah list all three things instead of just saying 'Leave'?
Three things left behind.right: To stress how much he was giving up
wrong: Because Avraham owned three separate houses
The list is about what leaving costs, not property.
Because each one was a separate journey
Because G-d wanted him to choose only one of them
He had to leave all three.
Three things left behind.exp: Listing each layer shows the size of the sacrifice.

Three things left behind.q: The three things move from wider to closer. Which order matches Genesis 12:1?
wrong: Father's house, then birthplace, then land, ending with the widest one
The verse goes from widest to closest.

Avraham's silence.q: What is missing from Avraham's response in Genesis 12:4?
wrong: Any mention that he actually left
The verse says he went forth.
The verse says he went as G-d commanded.
Avraham's silence.exp: He doesn't ask why, where, or what he will get. Class called it obedience, which could be good or bad.

Avraham's silence.q: Which best explains why historians must be careful with Avraham's silence?
Avraham's silence.right: Silence alone can't show what he felt
wrong: The text tells us exactly why Avraham went, so there is nothing left to infer
The text gives no inner reasons.
He argued with G-d at length
Avraham's silence.exp: Genesis 12:4 records only that he went.

Suggests vs. proves.q: Which statement goes beyond what Genesis 12:4 can prove?
Suggests vs. proves.right: Avraham felt no fear at all about leaving
wrong: Avraham left as G-d had commanded him to go
Avraham did not ask questions in the verse
Lot traveled with Avraham when he left Haran
Genesis 12:4 says Lot went with him.
Suggests vs. proves.exp: The text shows his action. His feelings are an inference.

Suggests vs. proves.q: Which claim is an INFERENCE rather than something Genesis 12:4 states?
wrong: Avraham went as G-d had commanded him, according to the verse
Suggests vs. proves.exp: His trust is suggested, not established, by the text.

Torah's silence on the choice.q: Based only on Genesis 12:1–4, what reason does the Torah give for choosing Avraham?
wrong: He was the most righteous man in Ur
He discovered G-d as a child in Ur
That idea comes from Rambam, not from Genesis 12.
He argued with G-d to save Sodom
Torah's silence on the choice.exp: The midrash and Rambam fill a gap the Torah leaves open.

Torah's silence on the choice.q: Which source tries to fill the gap the Torah leaves about why Avraham was chosen?
Torah's silence on the choice.right: Rambam's account of the child reasoning to one G-d
wrong: Genesis 12:4, which says that Abram went as G-d had commanded him to do
That describes his response, not why he was chosen.
Torah's silence on the choice.exp: Later sources like Rambam and the midrash offer reasons the Torah doesn't.

Bereishit Rabbah 39:1.q: In the palace parable, what does the owner looking out represent?
wrong: Avraham revealing himself to G-d in the palace
Avraham is the traveler who asks the question.
The people of Ur rejecting their idols
The parable is about one man's search.
Pharaoh welcoming Yaakov's family to Egypt
That is from the Joseph story.
Bereishit Rabbah 39:1.exp: Palace = the world; owner = G-d; traveler = Avraham.

Bereishit Rabbah 39:1.q: In the palace parable, what does the traveler's question suggest about Avraham?
Bereishit Rabbah 39:1.right: He searched for who was behind the world
wrong: He wanted to buy the palace and live in it with his family and servants
The parable is about seeking the owner.
He was afraid of the owner
Bereishit Rabbah 39:1.exp: Seeing the lit palace, he asks if it has no owner; then the owner looks out.

Rambam on Avraham.q: According to Rambam, how did Avraham come to believe in one G-d?
Rambam on Avraham.right: By questioning and reasoning on his own
wrong: By being taught by his father's teachers
Rambam says he had no teacher.
By hearing G-d speak at Mount Sinai
By copying the beliefs of the people of Ur
Rambam on Avraham.exp: Rambam: he wondered how the sphere could turn with no one controlling it.

Rambam on Avraham.q: How does Rambam's account differ from Genesis 12?
Rambam on Avraham.right: Rambam has Avraham find G-d first
wrong: Rambam says G-d chose Avraham for no reason, exactly as Genesis 12 does
Rambam gives a reason: his reasoning.
Rambam says Avraham had a teacher
Rambam places him in Canaan as a child
Rambam on Avraham.exp: In Rambam, Avraham reasons his way to one G-d; in Genesis 12, G-d simply speaks.

Who took the first step?.q: Which pair of sources best supports the position that Avraham and G-d chose each other?
wrong: Only Genesis 12, which shows Avraham searching first
Genesis 12 shows G-d speaking first, with no search.
Only Rambam, which says G-d called Avraham at birth
Exodus 1, which describes Pharaoh's fear of Israel
Exodus 1 is unrelated to Avraham's choice.
Who took the first step?.exp: Genesis 12: G-d calls. Midrash: Avraham searches and G-d answers.

Who took the first step?.q: Which source best supports the position that Avraham chose G-d?
wrong: Genesis 12, where G-d speaks first and gives Avraham a command to go forth
Who took the first step?.exp: Rambam: Avraham reasoned his way to G-d.

Belief alone isn't enough.q: If belief in one G-d is not enough on its own, what new element begins in Genesis 12?
wrong: A written law code for a nation
The law code comes at Sinai.
A king ruling over a nation
A temple in Jerusalem for worship
There is no temple in Genesis.
Belief alone isn't enough.exp: Genesis 12 adds mutual commitment to belief.

Belief alone isn't enough.q: Which example best supports the idea that belief alone isn't enough?
Belief alone isn't enough.right: A covenant brings obligations, like brit milah
wrong: Rambam's account of Avraham reasoning his way to one G-d as a young child
Belief alone isn't enough.exp: What begins in Genesis 12 is a covenant with obligations.

Why begin with Avraham.q: Which reason from your notes best explains why the course begins Jewish history with Avraham rather than Adam or Noah?
wrong: He was the first human being created
Adam and Eve were the first humans.
He was the first person to leave a city
The notes do not make this claim.
He received the Ten Commandments at Sinai
That was the whole people, generations later.
Why begin with Avraham.exp: Your notes: 'Maybe Avraham is the first Jew as he had a brit milah — the brit milah is the covenant.'

Why begin with Avraham.q: Why might the course begin with Avraham rather than earlier figures?
Why begin with Avraham.right: The covenant and brit milah begin with him
wrong: He was the first person in the Torah to believe in anything at all
Your notes point to the covenant, not belief.
Why begin with Avraham.exp: Your notes: the covenant and its sign begin with him.

Leaving Haran.q: Class notes call Avraham a 'sheep' in Genesis 12. Which reading of that story is best supported?
Leaving Haran.right: His obedience could be read as faith or as not thinking
wrong: He refused to leave until G-d explained the reason to him
He left only because Lot asked him to go
He left because G-d commanded him.
He argued that the trip was far too dangerous to make
Leaving Haran.exp: Class: obedience could be good or bad.

Leaving Haran.q: Which detail of Genesis 12 suggests Avraham did not go entirely alone?
wrong: He sent his servants ahead to find the land before he himself left Haran

Avraham and Lot.q: What does Avraham's offer to Lot most clearly show?
Avraham and Lot.right: He valued peace over getting the best land
wrong: He wanted the Jordan plain for himself
He was afraid of fighting his nephew's herdsmen
The text stresses peace between relatives, not fear.
He punished Lot for the quarrel
Avraham and Lot.exp: "Let there be no quarrel… for we are relatives." He could have taken the better land.

Avraham and Lot.q: Avraham's offer to Lot is best used as evidence of which trait?
Avraham and Lot.right: Peacemaking at a cost to himself
wrong: Greed, since he made sure to take the best land for his own herds first
Avraham and Lot.exp: He let Lot choose first to keep the peace.

Lot's choice.q: Which detail best supports the claim that Avraham gave up an advantage in Genesis 13?
wrong: Genesis 13 doesn't send him to Egypt.
That does not show a lost advantage.
Avraham and Lot were both wealthy
Wealth was the cause of the problem.
Lot's choice.exp: Letting Lot choose meant Avraham might get the worse land.

Lot's choice.q: What does Lot's choice of the well-watered Jordan plain suggest?
wrong: He chose the poorer land so that his uncle Avraham could have the best
Lot's choice.exp: Lot took the well-watered plain, and they separated.

Avraham pleads for Sodom.q: How does Avraham's response in Genesis 18 differ from Genesis 12?
Avraham pleads for Sodom.right: He questions G-d instead of obeying silently
wrong: He obeys silently, exactly as he did in Genesis 12
He argues for his own family's safety
He argues for strangers in Sodom.
He refuses to speak to G-d at all
Avraham pleads for Sodom.exp: Genesis 12: 'OK, I will go.' Genesis 18: 'What if there are innocents?'

Avraham pleads for Sodom.q: In Genesis 18, Avraham pleads for strangers. How does this compare with Genesis 12?
Avraham pleads for Sodom.right: He speaks up here but was silent in Genesis 12
wrong: He is silent and obedient in both stories without asking G-d any questions
Avraham pleads for Sodom.exp: Genesis 12: no questions. Genesis 18: he challenges G-d.

\"Shall not the Judge of all the earth d.q: What does this question assume about G-d?
wrong: That G-d has no power over Sodom
Avraham assumes G-d can destroy Sodom.
That Sodom's people were all innocent
He asks about fifty righteous among the wicked.
That G-d had already forgiven Sodom
He is arguing before any decision.
\"Shall not the Judge of all the earth d.exp: Avraham appeals to G-d's own justice.

\"Shall not the Judge of all the earth d.q: What does Avraham's question show about his relationship with G-d?
\"Shall not the Judge of all the earth d.right: He holds G-d to a standard of justice
wrong: He doubts that G-d exists and wants proof before he will believe anything
He asks about the righteous among the wicked.
\"Shall not the Judge of all the earth d.exp: He appeals to justice as something G-d upholds.

Hagar.q: Which statement about Avraham in the Hagar story is best supported by the text?
Hagar.right: He avoided taking responsibility in the conflict
wrong: He defended Hagar against Sarai's harsh treatment
He said, 'Your servant is in your hands.'
He argued with G-d for Hagar's sake
There is no argument with G-d here.
He sent Hagar away himself to protect Sarai's honor
Sarai treated her harshly and she ran away.
Hagar.exp: Unlike Sodom, he does not stand up for the vulnerable person here.

Hagar.q: Which reading of the Hagar story is best supported by Genesis 16:1–6?
wrong: Avraham defends Hagar strongly and refuses to let Sarai treat her harshly
He tells Sarai to do as she thinks best.
Hagar.exp: He tells Sarai to do as she thinks best, and Hagar flees.

Akeidat Yitzchak.q: Which detail best shows Avraham's readiness to obey in the Akeida?
Akeidat Yitzchak.right: He rose early the next morning
wrong: He argued with G-d to save his son
He did not argue here, unlike Sodom.
He refused to bring the knife or wood
He took the firestone and knife.
He asked Sarai for permission to go
The text records no such request.
Akeidat Yitzchak.exp: "So early the next morning, Avraham saddled his donkey."

wrong: Avraham refuses to go, and G-d chooses someone else to lead the people
He goes and binds his son.

\"Here I am\".q: What does Avraham's answer 'Here I am' most suggest?
wrong: Doubt about who was calling him
The phrase shows readiness, not doubt.
A refusal to listen to G-d
A plan to argue for Sodom
\"Here I am\".exp: It signals availability before he even hears the command.

\"Here I am\".q: Avraham answers 'Here I am' at the start of the Akeida. Which other moment shows similar readiness?
wrong: Pleading with G-d to spare the doomed city of Sodom for the righteous
Telling Sarai to deal with Hagar
\"Here I am\".exp: Hineni and going forth both show readiness to respond.

Sodom vs. Akeida tension.q: Which question best captures the tension between Genesis 18 and Genesis 22?
Sodom vs. Akeida tension.right: Why argue for strangers but not for his son?
wrong: Why did Lot choose the well-watered Jordan plain?
Why did the herdsmen quarrel over grazing land?
Why did Pharaoh fear the Israelites in Exodus 1?
Sodom vs. Akeida tension.exp: This was a 'question I still have' in your Unit 1 reflection.

Sodom vs. Akeida tension.q: Which statement best describes the tension?
Sodom vs. Akeida tension.right: He argues for strangers but not for his son
wrong: He argues for his son but not for the strangers who live in the city of Sodom
He doesn't argue in the Akeida.
Sodom vs. Akeida tension.exp: He challenges G-d for Sodom but stays silent at the Akeida.

Chosen but not perfect.q: Which pair of stories best supports the claim that Avraham was not perfect yet still chosen?
wrong: Leaving Haran and leaving Haran again
One story can't show both sides.
Lot and Sodom, which both show only flaws
Both show strengths: peacemaking and courage.
Chosen but not perfect.exp: Strength in one story, weakness in another.

Chosen but not perfect.q: Which story best shows a weakness in Avraham's character?
wrong: Avraham and Lot, where he lets his nephew choose the better land first
Chosen but not perfect.exp: In the Hagar story he avoids conflict, and Hagar flees.

Chosenness as responsibility.q: Which statement best matches your study guide's idea of chosenness?
Chosenness as responsibility.right: Being chosen means taking on duties
wrong: Being chosen means never making mistakes
The guide contrasts responsibility with perfection.
Being chosen means ruling over other peoples
Nothing in your sources says this.
Being chosen means G-d asks nothing in return
The covenant asks obligations of Avraham.
Chosenness as responsibility.exp: Moshe is your example: chosen even though he made a mistake.

Chosenness as responsibility.q: Which statement contradicts your study guide's idea of chosenness?
Chosenness as responsibility.right: Being chosen means being better than others
wrong: Being chosen means being given obligations to carry out and to pass down
Chosenness as responsibility.exp: Chosenness is responsibility, not superiority or perfection.

Moshe's mistake.q: Why is Moshe a useful example when asking whether someone can be chosen without being perfect?
Moshe's mistake.right: He led despite a costly mistake
wrong: He never made a single mistake as leader
He entered the land with the whole nation
His mistake kept him out of the land.
He was chosen only after he became perfect
He was chosen as a flawed person.
Moshe's mistake.exp: It supports 'chosen means responsible, not perfect.'

Moshe's mistake.q: How does Moshe's story support the claim about Avraham?
wrong: Both were perfect leaders who never made a single mistake in their lives
Moshe's mistake kept him from Israel.

Abrahamic religions.q: According to your family-tree chart, how does Islam connect itself to Avraham?
wrong: The Jewish people trace their line through Yitzchak and Yaakov.
Through Esau, the ancestor of Edom
Esau is Yitzchak's son, not the line Islam claims.
Through Lot, Avraham's nephew from Haran
Lot is not the line Islam claims.
Abrahamic religions.exp: The chart notes Muhammad is not in the Hebrew Bible; the link comes from later Islamic tradition.

Abrahamic religions.q: Which statement about the Abrahamic religions is supported by your chart?
wrong: Islam traces Muhammad through Yitzchak, the son bound in the Akeida
Only Judaism traces back to Avraham
Abrahamic religions.exp: Islam traces Muhammad through Yishmael, son of Avraham and Hagar.

National revelation.q: Your notes contrast a revelation seen by a whole nation with one given to a single person. Which event is the first kind?
National revelation.exp: Sinai was public, for all Israel.

National revelation.q: What contrast do your notes draw about Sinai?
National revelation.right: A whole people vs. one person receiving revelation
wrong: A private revelation to Moshe alone vs. a public one to all of Egypt
Sinai was to the whole people.
A written law vs. no law
National revelation.exp: Sinai was seen by the whole people, unlike traditions resting on one person.

Brit.q: Which situation is most like a brit?
Brit.right: Two sides each promise and each give
wrong: A ruler gives an order that only subjects obey
A person privately believes in one G-d
That is belief, not a two-sided agreement.
A merchant sells goods once and leaves
A brit is an ongoing relationship, not a one-time trade.
Brit.exp: Your answer: 'a push-pull relationship where both must give and take.'

Brit.q: Which feature makes a relationship a brit rather than an order?
Brit.right: Both sides commit and both receive
wrong: One side gives orders and the other side must obey them without question
Brit.exp: Both sides make commitments and both receive something.

Covenant vs. command.q: What turns G-d's words in Genesis 12 from a command into a covenant?
wrong: The people vote to accept it
Covenant vs. command.exp: Avraham must go; G-d binds Himself to promises.

Covenant vs. command.q: In Genesis 12, what does G-d commit to that turns a command into a covenant?
Covenant vs. command.right: Promises like making Avraham a great nation
wrong: Nothing, since G-d only tells Avraham to leave without offering anything
A set price for the land
Covenant vs. command.exp: G-d's promises (great nation, blessing, a great name) bind G-d too.

Covenant vs. simple deal.q: Which feature best separates the covenant from a simple deal?
wrong: Both sides receive something in return
It involves a promise of land
A deal could include land too.
It begins with a request to leave home
That does not make it different from a deal.
Covenant vs. simple deal.exp: It is built to extend to Avraham's descendants.

Covenant vs. simple deal.q: Which detail shows the covenant is not a one-time deal?
wrong: Avraham is paid in full the moment he arrives in the land of Canaan
Covenant vs. simple deal.exp: It's an ongoing relationship passed down (Sinai, Deuteronomy 27).

Avraham's obligation.q: Which is Avraham's side of the covenant in Genesis 12?
wrong: Building a nation and a homeland himself
Becoming a nation is G-d's promise.
Making his own name great among nations
G-d promises to make his name great.
Blessing the families of the earth by law
That is part of G-d's promises.

Avraham's obligation.q: What makes Avraham's side of the covenant costly?
Avraham's obligation.right: He gives up home and family for the unknown
wrong: He has to pay a large sum of silver to the rulers of the land of Canaan
Avraham's obligation.exp: He leaves land, birthplace and father's house.

Great nation.q: A student claims this promise was fulfilled the moment Avraham arrived in Canaan. Which detail best challenges that claim?
Great nation.right: Jacob's family was still only 70 people
wrong: Avraham left Haran when G-d commanded him
That does not address the size of his family.
Lot chose the well-watered Jordan plain
Lot's choice is not about nationhood.
Avraham argued for Sodom in Genesis 18
That is about justice, not numbers.
Great nation.exp: Generations later, Jacob's household entering Egypt numbered 70.

Great nation.q: Why couldn't the promise of a great nation be fulfilled in Avraham's lifetime?
Great nation.right: A nation takes generations to form
wrong: Because Avraham refused to go to Canaan, so G-d took the promise back

Make your name great.q: Which evidence would best support the claim that this promise has been fulfilled?
wrong: Lot chose the better land in Genesis 13
That is his obligation, not the promise.
Make your name great.exp: Avraham is known across Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

Make your name great.q: Which is the best evidence that 'make your name great' has come true?
Make your name great.right: Three religions trace back to Avraham
wrong: Avraham became the king of Ur after he returned from his journey to Canaan
Make your name great.exp: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all remember him.

You shall be a blessing.q: How does 'you shall be a blessing' differ from 'I will bless you'?
wrong: It is a command, not a promise
Both are promises in the verse.
It is only about wealth in Canaan
It is about Avraham's effect on others.
It is said to Lot, not Avraham
You shall be a blessing.exp: One blessing is received; the other is given to others.

You shall be a blessing.q: 'You shall be a blessing' adds which duty to the covenant?
wrong: Avraham should keep the blessing for his family and share it with no one
It's about being a blessing to others.
You shall be a blessing.exp: He and his descendants are to be a source of blessing to others.

All the families of the earth.q: Why does your reflection say the covenant is not just between Avraham and G-d?
All the families of the earth.right: It reaches all families and later generations
wrong: It was made with Pharaoh as a partner
Pharaoh is not part of it.
It was cancelled after the Akeida
It applied only to Lot's family and his herdsmen in the plain
All the families of the earth.exp: The covenant is built to extend beyond one man.

All the families of the earth.q: Which idea does Genesis 12:3 add to the covenant?
wrong: It limits the covenant to Avraham and Sarah alone and to no one else
All the families of the earth are named.
All the families of the earth.exp: All the families of the earth shall bless themselves by him.

Bless those who bless you.q: Which of G-d's promises in Genesis 12 is about how other peoples treat Avraham?
wrong: That is about his own descendants.
That is about his own fame.
Showing him a new land to live in
Bless those who bless you.exp: This promise concerns outsiders' behavior toward Avraham.

wrong: how Avraham should treat his own servants and the members of his household
It's about others' treatment of him.
Bless those who bless you.exp: 'I will bless those who bless you and curse the one who curses you.'

Uneven trade.q: What makes the Genesis 12 exchange look uneven on paper?
Uneven trade.right: One act now, many promises later
wrong: G-d asks for much more than He promises
G-d promises more than one thing.
The promises come true over generations.
Uneven trade.exp: That is why the covenant requires trust.

Uneven trade.q: Why might the exchange in Genesis 12 seem uneven?
Uneven trade.right: One costly act now; promises over generations
wrong: Avraham promises many things over generations while G-d does one thing now
Both sides give exactly the same
Uneven trade.exp: Avraham's side is one act now; G-d's side unfolds over time.

Brit milah.q: Why might brit milah matter more than belief alone in making Avraham 'the first Jew'?
wrong: It was required of everyone in Ur
It replaced the promise of land
Land remained part of the covenant.
Brit milah.exp: Your notes: 'brit milah / bris is the covenant.'

Brit milah.q: How is brit milah different from belief?
Brit milah.right: It's a physical sign of the covenant
wrong: It's a private thought that no one else can see or check in any way
It's a prayer said once a year
Brit milah.exp: Circumcision is the covenant's physical sign.

Covenant of the pieces.q: According to your notes, what did G-d tell Avraham would happen before his descendants received the land?
Covenant of the pieces.right: They would be slaves in a foreign land
wrong: They would conquer Egypt by force
They would be enslaved, not conquer.
They would rule Mesopotamia from Ur
They would receive the land immediately
There would be a long wait first.
Covenant of the pieces.exp: Your answer links this to the years in Egypt.

Covenant of the pieces.q: What does Genesis 15 tell Avraham about his descendants' future?
wrong: Immediate kingship in Canaan with no hardship along the way
Covenant of the pieces.exp: Strangers and slaves in a foreign land, then a return (about 400 years).

Genesis 15:16.q: Which explanation of the long wait is stated in Genesis 15:16?
Genesis 15:16.right: The Amorites' wrongdoing was not yet complete
wrong: The Israelites had not yet learned to farm the land
Pharaoh refused to let Joseph's family go
Avraham had disobeyed G-d in Haran by asking questions
Genesis 15:16.exp: This is what the Torah says; a historian might infer other reasons.

Genesis 15:16.q: According to Genesis 15:16, why must the return wait?
Genesis 15:16.right: The Amorites' iniquity is not yet complete
wrong: Avraham's descendants are not yet strong enough to defeat the Egyptians
The verse gives a different reason.
Genesis 15:16.exp: 'For the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.'

Righteousness and justice.q: Why does passing righteousness and justice to future generations matter for the covenant?
Righteousness and justice.right: The covenant depends on later generations keeping it
wrong: It lets each generation ignore the covenant
The covenant asks each generation to carry it.
It ended the covenant after Avraham died
It means only Avraham himself was responsible for keeping the covenant
Righteousness and justice.exp: Your notes: responsibility for Avraham's descendants — 10 commandments, 613 mitzvot, passing down beliefs.

Righteousness and justice.q: Which later event best shows righteousness and justice being passed down?
Righteousness and justice.right: The covenant at Sinai with its obligations
wrong: Lot choosing the well-watered plain of the Jordan for his own herds
Righteousness and justice.exp: Duties begun with Avraham pass to the whole people at Sinai.

Covenant at Sinai.q: What is one major change from the covenant with Avraham to the covenant at Sinai?
Covenant at Sinai.right: A whole people accepts it together
wrong: It no longer involves any promises
Sinai includes promises such as 'treasured possession.'
It is made with Pharaoh instead of Israel
It drops all of the conditions and duties
Covenant at Sinai.exp: Avraham: an individual. Sinai: a nation, with laws.

Covenant at Sinai.q: Which word in 'if you obey My voice' shows the covenant at Sinai has conditions?
wrong: Voice, because it shows that G-d spoke out loud to the people at the mountain
Covenant at Sinai.exp: 'If you obey… and keep My covenant': the promises depend on the people's choice.

Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.q: What does 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' suggest about the Israelites' status at Sinai?
Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.right: They are a nation before entering the land
wrong: They have become slaves again in Egypt
They will only become a family much later
They have already conquered Canaan by the time it is said
They are still in the wilderness.
Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.exp: Your answer used this as evidence they were a nation before the land.

Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.q: What does 'kingdom of priests' suggest about Israel's role?
Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.right: A whole people set apart for a special role
wrong: Only priests would count as members of the people and everyone else is excluded
Israel would be ruled by Egypt
Kingdom of priests and a holy nation.exp: The whole nation is to be holy if they keep the covenant.

Naaseh v'Nishmah.q: Why was saying 'we will do' first significant?
Naaseh v'Nishmah.right: It showed commitment to act on the laws
wrong: It showed the laws were forced on them
It meant only the leaders agreed to it
It showed they rejected the covenant offered at Sinai
Naaseh v'Nishmah.exp: A shared choice to act, made as one people.

Naaseh v'Nishmah.q: What does 'with one voice' add to Naaseh v'Nishmah?
wrong: Only Moshe answered on behalf of the people, who stayed silent
Naaseh v'Nishmah.exp: The people answered together: we will do and we will obey.

Deuteronomy 27:9–10.q: Why does Moshe renew the covenant with the next generation?
Deuteronomy 27:9–10.right: Each generation must accept it for itself
wrong: The first covenant had been cancelled
He wanted to replace the Torah's laws
He tells them to obey the commandments.
They had already entered the land and needed new rules
Deuteronomy 27:9–10.exp: Nationhood and covenant must be renewed, not simply inherited.

Deuteronomy 27:9–10.q: Why renew the covenant forty years after Sinai?
Deuteronomy 27:9–10.right: A new generation must accept it
wrong: The old covenant had been canceled because the people broke it at Sinai
Deuteronomy 27:9–10.exp: 'This day you have become the people of the Lord': each generation takes it on.

Guilt vs. responsibility.q: Ten people hear an antisemitic joke and no one responds. What does the Yom Kippur lesson say about the listeners?
wrong: They are guilty of telling the joke
They didn't tell it, so it isn't guilt.
They have no role since it wasn't theirs
Only the teacher can ever respond
Guilt vs. responsibility.exp: Covenant = I belong; responsibility = my belonging asks something of me.

Guilt vs. responsibility.q: Which statement best matches the Yom Kippur lesson?
Guilt vs. responsibility.right: You can be responsible without being guilty
wrong: You are only responsible for problems that you yourself caused directly
Guilt and responsibility are the same
Guilt vs. responsibility.exp: You may not have caused it and still be responsible for what happens next.

Teshuvah.q: How does teshuvah connect to the idea that chosenness is not perfection?
Teshuvah.right: It expects mistakes and asks for repair
wrong: It means a chosen person never errs
It replaces the covenant with feelings of guilt
It moves from guilt to action.
It applies only to the people of Ur
It is a Yom Kippur idea for everyone.
Teshuvah.exp: Falling short is expected; returning and repairing is the duty.

Teshuvah.q: How does teshuvah fit with chosenness as responsibility?
wrong: It means a chosen person never fails, so repair is never needed
Teshuvah.exp: 'I will sometimes fall short. I can return, repair and act.'

Ways to step up.q: You see a classmate bullied and you can't stop it in the moment. Which option from the lesson is still a way to step up?
Ways to step up.right: Bring in someone better positioned to help
wrong: Do nothing, since noticing is enough
The lesson says noticing isn't the same as acting.
Join in so the bully stops targeting you instead
Wait until it becomes your own problem
Belonging makes it yours to care about.
Ways to step up.exp: 'Involve' is one of the five ways.

Ways to step up.q: Which is an example of 'involve' from the list?
Ways to step up.right: Telling a teacher who can help
wrong: Stepping in to stop the comment yourself right when it happens
Ways to step up.exp: Involve means bringing in someone who can help.

Terah.q: Who heads the family-tree chart 'From Terah to the 12 Tribes'?
wrong: Avraham's nephew who went with him

Terah.q: Which pair were both sons of Terah?
wrong: Yitzchak and Yishmael, the two sons born to Avraham by different mothers
Terah.exp: Terah was father of Avraham, Nahor and Haran.

Lot.q: Why does Avraham say 'we are relatives' to Lot in Genesis 13?
wrong: Lot is his son by Hagar
The chart shows Lot as Haran's son.
Lot is one of Yaakov's sons
Lot.exp: Lot is the son of Avraham's brother Haran.

Lot.q: How was Lot related to Avraham?
Lot.right: Nephew: son of Avraham's brother Haran
wrong: Son: born to Avraham and Sarah before Yitzchak, their younger child
Lot.exp: Lot was the son of Avraham's brother Haran.

Yishmael.q: Which son of Avraham does the chart connect to later Islamic tradition?
wrong: The Jewish line goes through Yitzchak.
Esau is the ancestor of Edom.
Avraham and Sarah, who also had Yitzchak when they were very old
Their sons were Esau and Yaakov.
Yishmael.exp: Yishmael was the son of Avraham and Hagar the Egyptian.

Yitzchak.q: Through which son of Avraham do the Jewish people trace their line?
wrong: Islam traces its line through Yishmael.
Lot's choice of the well-watered Jordan plain after the herdsmen quarreled
Yitzchak.exp: Yitzchak is the son bound in the Akeida.

Esau.q: Which son of Yitzchak is NOT the ancestor of the 12 tribes?
wrong: Yaakov is the father of the 12 tribes.
Joseph is a grandson, not Yitzchak's son.
Levi is a grandson, not Yitzchak's son.

Esau.q: Which people does Esau's line become?
wrong: The Israelites, through his twin brother's twelve sons and their tribes
Esau.exp: Esau is ancestor of the Edomites.

Yaakov.q: Why are his descendants called 'the Israelites'?
wrong: Avraham was renamed Israel at Sinai
The name Israel belongs to Yaakov.
His sons were Manasseh and Ephraim.
Pharaoh gave them the name in Egypt
Yaakov.exp: Children of Israel = children of Yaakov.

Yaakov.q: Which name of Yaakov's became the name of the people?
wrong: Edom, the name his twin brother's descendants came to be known by
Yaakov.exp: Yaakov was also named Israel; his descendants are the Israelites.

Leah.q: Your notes say Yaakov loved Rachel but was tricked. Who did he marry first?
wrong: Rivka, Yitzchak's wife and Yaakov's mother

Leah.q: Which tribe ancestor was a son of Leah?
wrong: Joseph, the son who later rose to power in Egypt and saved his family
Leah.exp: Leah's sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun (and daughter Dinah).

Rachel.q: Which two sons were born to Yaakov's beloved wife?
wrong: Dan and Naphtali, born to her servant

Rachel.q: How were Leah and Rachel related?
wrong: Mother and daughter, since Rachel was Leah's daughter from an earlier marriage

Bilhah.q: Dan and Naphtali were born to which woman?
wrong: Leah bore six sons, not these two.
Leah's, who gave her to Yaakov so that she could have more sons of her own
Bilhah.exp: Bilhah was Rachel's servant, mother of Dan and Naphtali.

Zilpah.q: Gad and Asher were born to which woman?
Which pair of mothers and sons is correct?
wrong: Zilpah: Dan and Naphtali, who were born while Rachel still had no children
Zilpah.exp: Zilpah, Leah's servant, bore Gad and Asher.

The 12 sons.q: Which name on the chart is NOT one of Yaakov's 12 sons?
wrong: Levi is one of Leah's sons.
Asher is one of Zilpah's sons.
Benjamin is one of Rachel's sons.
The 12 sons.exp: Dinah is Yaakov's daughter; the 12 tribes come from his sons.

The 12 sons.q: Why do the 12 sons matter for the story of a nation?
The 12 sons.right: They became the ancestors of the 12 tribes
wrong: They were the twelve kings of Egypt who ruled in turn after Joseph died
The 12 sons.exp: Yaakov's 12 sons are the ancestors of the 12 tribes.

Manasseh and Ephraim.q: Genesis 46 counts 70 people in Yaakov's household, including two born in Egypt. Who were they?
wrong: They are not part of Yaakov's household.
Manasseh and Ephraim.exp: "Joseph's sons who were born to him in Egypt were two in number."

Manasseh and Ephraim.q: Where were Manasseh and Ephraim born?
wrong: In Canaan, before Yaakov's family went down to Egypt during the famine
Manasseh and Ephraim.exp: Joseph's two sons were born in Egypt; Manasseh was firstborn.

Family.q: At what stage does Genesis 46 describe Yaakov's household entering Egypt?
wrong: A nation with its own land and laws
It had no land or government of its own.
A kingdom of priests at Sinai
Family.exp: "All the persons belonging to Jacob… 70 persons."

Family.q: Which best describes Yaakov's household when it entered Egypt?
wrong: A nation with its own land, laws and government already in place in Egypt
They had no land or government.

People.q: Which evidence best shows the Israelites had become a people by Exodus 1?
wrong: That is when they were still a family.
They received laws at Mount Sinai
Sinai helps make them a nation, later.
They crossed the Jordan River into the land of Canaan
People.exp: Outsiders now see a distinct group, not just Yaakov's family.

People.q: What separates a people from a family?
People.right: Many families sharing history and values
wrong: Having its own land, laws and government that rule over its own territory
People.exp: A people is many families with a shared history, values and background.

Nation.q: By Exodus 1, what were the Israelites still missing to be a nation?
wrong: Those made them a people already.
A name used by outsiders such as Pharaoh
Pharaoh already called them a people.
Nation.exp: Your answer: a people, but not yet a nation.

Nation.q: Which event in Lesson 2.3 gave the Israelites the last piece of nationhood?
wrong: Leaving Egypt, which first gave them freedom from slavery under Pharaoh
Nation.exp: A nation also has land; entering Canaan completed it.

70 persons.q: Why does the number 70 matter when comparing Genesis 46 and Exodus 1?
70 persons.right: It shows how small they began
wrong: It shows Egypt had only 70 people
It counts the years of slavery
It counts the laws given at Sinai
70 persons.exp: From 70 people to a population that 'filled the land.'

70 persons.q: How does the shift from '70 persons' to 'the Israelite people' show change over time?
70 persons.right: A small family grew into a people
wrong: A large nation shrank into a single family after many years of slavery
70 persons.exp: From 70 persons (Genesis 46) to a people that filled the land (Exodus 1).

Fertile and prolific.q: Which phrase from Exodus 1:7 best shows growth?
wrong: That is about Pharaoh, not growth.
That is about a death, not growth.
"his own issue aside from the wives"
Fertile and prolific.exp: Growth turned a family into a large, distinct group.

Fertile and prolific.q: How did the Israelites' growth in Exodus 1:7 lead to Pharaoh's fear?
Fertile and prolific.right: Their numbers made them seem a threat
wrong: Their growth made Pharaoh want to give them more land and power in Egypt
Fertile and prolific.exp: 'Too numerous… they may join our enemies.'

Joseph rations the grain.q: Why was Egypt a place of salvation during the famine?
Joseph rations the grain.right: Joseph had stored and rationed grain
wrong: Egypt had no famine that year
Pharaoh refused to sell any grain at all
Canaan had more food than Egypt did
Yaakov's family came to Egypt for food.
Joseph rations the grain.exp: Egypt had bread because of Joseph's planning.

Joseph rations the grain.q: Why did 'the whole world' come to Egypt?
Joseph rations the grain.right: Joseph had stored grain for the famine
wrong: Egypt had conquered the world and forced every people to bring tribute
Joseph rations the grain.exp: Joseph opened the storehouses during the famine.

\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".q: How does Joseph interpret his brothers selling him into slavery?
\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".right: As part of G-d's plan to save lives
wrong: As proof his brothers were righteous
As a reason to punish them severely
He tells them not to be distressed.
As a sign to return to Canaan at once
He brings the family to Egypt.
\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".exp: "You intended me harm, G-d intended it for good."

\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".q: Joseph's words to his brothers best show which idea?
\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".right: A larger purpose behind a painful event
wrong: Revenge against his brothers for selling him into slavery in Egypt
He says G-d sent him to save life.
That his brothers did nothing wrong
He reframes it, not excuses it.
\"G-d sent me ahead of you\".exp: 'It was not you but G-d': sent to save life.

Goshen.q: Which detail from Genesis 47:27 best explains why the family might not want to leave Egypt?
wrong: They were slaves in Goshen right away
Slavery came later, under a new king.
Goshen was in Canaan, not Egypt
They were forbidden to own anything

Goshen.q: What happened to Yaakov's family in Goshen?
Goshen.right: They acquired holdings and grew greatly
wrong: They were enslaved right away by the new Pharaoh who did not know Joseph
Goshen.exp: Settled near Joseph, acquired holdings, grew greatly.

Why they stayed.q: Which pair gives one practical and one covenant reason the family stayed in Egypt?
Why they stayed.right: Fertile land; waiting for G-d's notice
wrong: Fear of Pharaoh; love of the pyramids
Slavery came later; the commandments came at Sinai.
Avraham's order; Lot's choice of the Jordan plain
Why they stayed.exp: Your answer: fertile land, Joseph's power; and 'pakod yifkod.'

Why they stayed.q: Which reason for staying in Egypt is a covenant reason?
Why they stayed.right: Waiting for G-d to bring them out
wrong: The land of Goshen was fertile and they prospered there under Joseph
Why they stayed.exp: Covenant reason: waiting for G-d (pakod yifkod).

Pakod yifkod.q: How might pakod yifkod have encouraged later generations to stay in Egypt?
Pakod yifkod.right: They waited for G-d to bring them out
wrong: It ordered them to leave immediately
It promised G-d would act in the future.
It said Egypt was the promised land
It told them to fight Pharaoh's army for their freedom
It is about waiting for G-d.
Pakod yifkod.exp: Leaving might have been seen as G-d's timing, not theirs.

Pakod yifkod.q: Pakod yifkod connects to which earlier promise?
Pakod yifkod.right: The land promised to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov
wrong: The promise to Hagar that her son would be the father of a great nation
Pakod yifkod.exp: G-d would bring them up to the land promised to the patriarchs.

Joseph's bones.q: What does Joseph's request about his bones show he expected?
wrong: That Egypt would be home forever
He wanted his bones moved out.
That he would be buried in Goshen
He asked to be carried up from Egypt.
That his brothers would stay as slaves
He expected G-d to bring them out.
Joseph's bones.exp: He expected G-d to bring them back to the land promised to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov.

Joseph's bones.q: Joseph's request is best used as evidence that he
Joseph's bones.right: expected his people to return to the land
wrong: expected his family to stay in Egypt forever and become fully Egyptian
He wanted his bones carried up.
He trusted G-d would take notice.
Joseph's bones.exp: 'You shall carry up my bones from here.'

Yaakov's burial request.q: What do Yaakov's and Joseph's burial requests have in common?
Yaakov's burial request.right: Both point to Canaan as home
wrong: Both ask to be buried in Goshen
Both reject the covenant with Avraham
Both are made after leaving Egypt
Yaakov's burial request.exp: Even while prospering in Egypt, they saw Canaan as the promised home.

Yaakov's burial request.q: Where did Yaakov ask to be buried?
Yaakov's burial request.right: The cave of Machpelah in Canaan
wrong: In Goshen, near his son Joseph and the rest of the family in Egypt
He asked not to be left in Egypt.
Yaakov's burial request.exp: With his ancestors in the cave of Machpelah.

400 years.q: A historian says famine and prosperity explain the long stay in Egypt. What kind of statement is this compared with Genesis 15:16?
400 years.right: An inference, not what the Torah says
wrong: A direct quote from the Torah
Something we can observe today in Egypt
A rejection of all the evidence
400 years.exp: Torah says / we can observe / historians may infer.

400 years.q: Which source explains the long stay as part of a plan, not just famine?
wrong: Genesis 41, which describes Joseph rationing the grain during the famine years
That explains coming, not the long stay.
400 years.exp: G-d foretold the long stay to Avraham.

A new king who did not know Joseph.q: Why does it matter that the new king 'did not know Joseph'?
wrong: He had never heard of Egypt
He wanted to make Joseph's family rulers
He saw them as a threat.
A new king who did not know Joseph.exp: Joseph's power had protected them; now that link was broken.

A new king who did not know Joseph.q: 'Did not know Joseph' is the turning point because
wrong: the new king had never heard of Egypt and had just arrived from abroad
A new king who did not know Joseph.exp: With Joseph forgotten, the Israelites lost their protection.

Pharaoh's fear.q: What cause does Pharaoh give for treating the Israelites harshly?
Pharaoh's fear.right: Their growth might make them a threat in war
wrong: They refused to work the land
Religion is not his stated reason.
They had stolen grain from Egypt's storehouses during the famine
Grain is not his stated reason.
Pharaoh's fear.exp: Population growth plus fear of disloyalty.

Pharaoh's fear.q: Which phrase best shows Pharaoh viewing the Israelites as a separate people?
wrong: 'G-d sent me ahead of you,' which Joseph said to his brothers in Egypt
'We will do and we will obey'
Pharaoh's fear.exp: He sees them as a group with its own loyalty.

Leaving Egypt.q: Why might leaving Egypt come first on any list of nation-building events?
wrong: That came with entering the land.
It gave them the Ten Commandments
It ended the covenant with Avraham
Leaving Egypt.exp: Your answer: freedom had to come first.

Leaving Egypt.q: What did leaving Egypt give the Israelites?
wrong: Their own land, laws and government on the day that they left Egypt

Crossing the sea.q: Which effect of crossing the sea did your answer stress?
Crossing the sea.right: It ended any return to Egypt
wrong: It gave them manna to eat every day
Crossing the sea.exp: It also united them in belief in G-d and Moshe.

Crossing the sea.q: According to Exodus 14, how did the people respond after crossing?
Crossing the sea.right: They believed in the Lord and in Moses
wrong: They asked to go back to Egypt because they feared the desert ahead
Crossing the sea.exp: 'And they believed in the Lord and in Moses.'

Manna.q: Why did your answer rank manna as contributing least to nationhood?
Manna.right: It helped them survive but added no new national feature
wrong: It caused the people to leave Egypt
It gave them their laws and covenant
It made them slaves again under a new and harsher Pharaoh
Manna.exp: An event can matter even if it ranks last.

Manna.q: What did manna teach the people?
Manna.right: To rely on G-d together each day
wrong: To store up as much food as possible for the long years ahead
Manna.exp: Bread from heaven each day taught shared reliance on G-d.

Ten Commandments.q: Which characteristic of a nation did the Ten Commandments add?
wrong: That came with entering the land.

Ten Commandments.q: Which feature of a nation did the Ten Commandments provide?
wrong: Land, which the people received when they crossed the Jordan River

Mishkan.q: What did building the Mishkan add to the Israelites' nationhood?
Mishkan.right: A central place of worship they built together
wrong: A permanent capital city in Canaan
The Mishkan was carried through the wilderness.
Their escape from Pharaoh's army at the sea of Reeds
Mishkan.exp: A shared project and shared worship.

Mishkan.q: What made building the Mishkan a shared nation-building act?
Mishkan.right: The people built it together for worship
wrong: Moshe built it alone in secret while the people waited at the camp
Mishkan.exp: 'That I may dwell among them': shared worship.

Entering the land.q: Your answer says the land 'completed their nationhood but did not create it.' Which evidence supports that?
Entering the land.right: They were called a nation at Sinai
wrong: They had no laws before entering
That supports 'people,' not the timing of nationhood.
They crossed the Jordan on dry ground
That describes entering, not prior nationhood.
Entering the land.exp: 'A kingdom of priests and a holy nation' was said in the wilderness.

Entering the land.q: Who crossed the Jordan into Canaan in Joshua 3?
wrong: The same generation that left Egypt, only a few weeks after the sea crossing
It was a new generation after 40 years.
Entering the land.exp: After 40 years a new generation crossed the Jordan.

Nationhood as a process.q: Which statement is the best-supported conclusion about when the Israelites became a nation?
wrong: Sinai already called them a nation.
Freedom alone gave no laws or land.
Only when Joseph became powerful in Egypt
They were still a family then.

Nationhood as a process.q: Which order matches the process in your notes?
Nationhood as a process.right: Freedom, law and covenant, worship, land
wrong: Land first, then worship, then law and covenant, and freedom at the very end
Nationhood as a process.exp: Freedom, then law and covenant, then shared worship, then land.

Antisemitism.q: Which example best fits hostility toward Jews as Jews?
Antisemitism.right: Blaming all Jews for a government's actions
wrong: Criticizing one Israeli policy with evidence
Criticizing a policy is not hostility toward Jews as Jews.
Voting for a party in the Knesset
Antisemitism.exp: The key is targeting Jews for being Jews.

Antisemitism.q: Which example is NOT antisemitism under your class definition?
wrong: Blaming Jews as a group for a problem simply because they are Jewish
That is hostility to Jews as Jews.
Claiming Jews are a dangerous race
Antisemitism.exp: Criticizing a policy differs from hostility to Jews for being Jewish.

Criticism vs. hostility.q: A protester says, 'I oppose this Israeli policy.' Another says, 'Jews everywhere are to blame.' What separates them?
Criticism vs. hostility.right: The second targets Jews as a group
wrong: Criticizing a policy is not automatically antisemitic.
Both are equally just political criticism
The second blames Jews as Jews.
The second targets Jews as a group.
Criticism vs. hostility.exp: Your note: supporting Palestinians doesn't by itself mean hostility to Jews.

Criticism vs. hostility.q: Which question best helps decide whether a statement is antisemitic?
Criticism vs. hostility.right: Is it aimed at a policy or at Jews as Jews?
wrong: Was it said loudly or quietly, and did many people hear it at the time?
Is it about the Middle East?
Criticism vs. hostility.exp: The key test: a policy, or Jews for being Jewish.

Racial antisemitism.q: What made the Nazi view of Jews different from objecting to a religion?
Racial antisemitism.right: It claimed Jewishness could never change
wrong: It said Jews could convert to escape it
It claimed it could not be changed.
It only criticized a government policy
It targeted Jews as a so-called race.
It praised Jews as a superior people of the world
It called them inferior and dangerous.
Racial antisemitism.exp: Racial antisemitism makes Jewishness a permanent label.

Racial antisemitism.q: Why couldn't a Jew escape Nazi racial antisemitism by converting?
wrong: Conversion was illegal in every European country during the Nazi period
The Nazis only targeted religious practice
Racial antisemitism.exp: Hitler claimed Jewishness was an unchangeable race.

Overgeneralization.q: Which statement is an overgeneralization from your true/false review?
Overgeneralization.right: Everyone at a pro-Palestinian protest supports Hamas
wrong: Some extremists can pose a serious risk to a community
That is limited and was marked true.
Not all Muslims are Arab, according to your class review

Overgeneralization.right: Some members of a group hold a view
wrong: Everyone at a protest supports whatever the most extreme person there says
Overgeneralization.exp: Claims about some shouldn't be stretched to all.

Most Muslims are not Arab.q: Which statement from your review was marked FALSE?
wrong: Both the Torah and Quran contain passages about war
A tiny share of extremists can still be dangerous
That is the corrected version, which is true.
Most Muslims are not Arab.exp: Arab is an ethnic and language group; Muslim is a religion.

Most Muslims are not Arab.q: What does 'Most Muslims are Arab' being false show?
Most Muslims are not Arab.right: Religion and ethnicity aren't the same
wrong: That there are no Arab Muslims anywhere in the world, only non-Arab ones
Most Muslims are not Arab.exp: Muslim (religion) and Arab (ethnicity) are different categories.

Not all Palestinians are Muslim.q: Why is 'All Palestinians are Muslim' a weak claim?
Not all Palestinians are Muslim.right: It turns a group into one religion
wrong: It is a fact recorded in the Torah
The Torah says nothing of this.
It is supported by your review sheet
Not all Palestinians are Muslim.exp: The word 'all' makes it an overgeneralization.

Not all Palestinians are Muslim.q: Which word makes 'All Palestinians are Muslim' easy to disprove?
wrong: Palestinians, because the word refers to a place rather than to a group of people

Small groups, serious risk.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the 0.1% statement?
Small groups, serious risk.right: A small group can still be dangerous
wrong: Most people in that population are extremists
Small groups can never cause real harm
The whole population must be blamed
Small groups, serious risk.exp: Size of a group and size of its danger are different questions.

Small groups, serious risk.q: Which pair of review statements together shows careful thinking?
Small groups, serious risk.right: Not everyone supports extremism, yet a few can pose risk
wrong: Everyone at a protest supports extremism, so the whole group is dangerous
No one supports extremism, so there is no risk
A small group can still pose risk.
Small groups, serious risk.exp: Avoid overgeneralizing while still recognizing a small group's risk.

Violence in scripture.q: A classmate says only one religion's scripture mentions war. What is the best response based on your review?
Violence in scripture.right: Both the Torah and Quran contain such passages
wrong: Neither text ever mentions any war
The review marked that both do.
Only the Torah discusses fighting and war of any kind
Violence in scripture.exp: Compare sources fairly before drawing conclusions.

Violence in scripture.q: What is the best use of the 'violence in scripture' fact?
Violence in scripture.right: To avoid singling out one religion unfairly
wrong: To prove that every religion's followers are violent people by nature
To show only the Quran mentions war
To show only the Torah mentions war

Checking a claim.q: A post says, 'The deadliest attacks on U.S. synagogues were all by Islamic extremists.' Your review marked this false. What should you check first?
Checking a claim.right: Who actually carried out each attack
wrong: Whether the post has many likes
Whether it uses the word 'synagogue' in the headline
Checking a claim.exp: Check the evidence behind each claim.

Checking a claim.q: A post says 'everyone' in a group believes something. What should you ask first?
Checking a claim.right: Does it apply to all or only some?
wrong: How many people have already shared the post with their friends online
Checking a claim.exp: Who made it, what's the evidence, and does it apply to all or only some?

Ottoman rule.q: Who controlled the land before World War I?
wrong: They became involved after World War I.
It came after World War I.

Ottoman rule.q: Which event ended Ottoman rule over the land?
wrong: The founding of the League of Nations' mandate system before the war began
Ottoman rule.exp: Ottoman control lasted 1517–1917; the empire fell in WWI.

Mandate system.q: What was the stated purpose of the mandate system?
Mandate system.right: To help a people become able to self-govern
wrong: To make the land part of Britain forever
It was meant to prepare self-rule.
To return the land to the Ottomans
To divide Europe among the winners after the war ended
Mandate system.exp: Your notes: 'we are going to help them set up.'

Mandate system.q: Who set up the mandate system?
wrong: The Ottoman Empire, which handed its lands to Britain and France in 1517
Mandate system.exp: After WWI the League of Nations set up mandates.

Partition.q: According to your notes, how did each side respond to the split?
Partition.right: Jews accepted it; Arabs rejected it
wrong: Both sides accepted the split gladly
Your notes say Arabs rejected it.
Your notes say Jews accepted it.
Jews rejected it; Arabs accepted it
Partition.exp: Your notes call it 'a very bad deal for Jews but they accepted.'

Partition.q: Why was partition proposed, according to your notes?
wrong: Because the Ottomans wanted to keep half of the land for themselves
Partition.exp: Arab–Jewish conflict led to the plan to split the land.

Knesset.q: How many seats does a party need to govern alone in the Knesset?
wrong: Half is not a majority; 61 is.
Knesset.exp: A majority is more than half: 61.

Knesset.q: A party has 50 seats. Can it govern alone?
wrong: Yes, because 50 seats is more than any other party has in the Knesset
Most seats isn't enough; 61 is needed.
Knesset.exp: The Knesset has 120 seats; a majority is 61.

Parliamentary democracy.q: Which statement about Israel's government is true according to your quick check?
wrong: It is ruled by a powerful president
Voters choose the prime minister directly
Parliamentary democracy.exp: You got this one right on the quick check.

Parliamentary democracy.q: In Israel's system, what does a government need to stay in power?
Parliamentary democracy.right: The support of a Knesset majority
wrong: The approval of the president, who can remove any government at any time
A direct vote for prime minister
Parliamentary democracy.exp: The government needs a Knesset majority.

Voting for a party.q: What do Israelis choose on the ballot in national elections?
wrong: The president isn't elected by the public.
They vote for a party list.
Voting for a party.exp: Seats are divided based on each party's share of the vote.

Voting for a party.q: Why can't an Israeli voter choose a prime minister directly on the ballot?
wrong: Prime ministers are appointed for life by the Knesset after one election
Voting for a party.exp: Israelis vote for a party list.

Israel's president.q: On your quick check you missed this one. Which statement is TRUE?
Israel's president.right: The president appoints who will try to form a government
wrong: The president runs the government day to day
The president controls the Knesset and decides which laws it passes
The president does not control the Knesset.
Israel's president.exp: Ceremonial role, with one key job after elections.

Israel's president.q: What real power does Israel's mainly ceremonial president have after an election?
Israel's president.right: Choosing who first tries to form a government
wrong: Commanding the army and writing the budget without the Knesset's approval
Israel's president.exp: The president appoints the person who will try to form a government.

Electoral threshold.q: A small party wins 2% of the vote. What happens?
wrong: It is not in the Knesset.
Electoral threshold.exp: A party that passes the threshold gets about 4 seats, not 1.

Electoral threshold.q: Why does the threshold matter for coalitions?
Electoral threshold.right: It keeps very small parties out
wrong: It guarantees that every party gets at least one seat in the Knesset
Electoral threshold.exp: About 3.25% is needed to enter the Knesset.

Coalition.q: Why do Israeli parties usually need to form coalitions?
Coalition.right: No single party controls a majority
wrong: Every party must be in the government
Some parties are in the opposition.
The president orders several parties to rule
The president doesn't choose the coalition.
Israel does not allow single-party rule by law
Coalition.exp: No party has ever won 61 seats alone.

Coalition.q: Parties A (30), B (20) and C (8) agree to govern together. Can they form a government?
wrong: Yes, because three parties working together always make a government

Opposition.q: After a coalition forms with 64 seats, what are the remaining parties called?
wrong: The president is not a party leader.
That is not a term for parties outside government.

Opposition.q: What role does the opposition play?
wrong: The parties that hold the most ministries and run the government each day

Largest party may not govern.q: Likud wins the most seats, 27, but cannot reach 61 with partners. What is the best-supported outcome?
Largest party may not govern.right: Another leader may get a chance to form a government
wrong: The Knesset is dissolved forever and never meets again after that
If no one succeeds, there are new elections.
Largest party may not govern.exp: Your notes: if the first can't, the second gets to try; if that fails, re-elections.

Largest party may not govern.q: Why might the second-largest party end up governing?
Largest party may not govern.right: It may build 61 seats when the largest can't
wrong: The second-largest party always governs by law in Israel's system
The president dislikes the largest party
Largest party may not govern.exp: Only a 61-seat coalition can govern; another leader may try.

Bloc.q: Your election tracker showed no bloc at 61. What does that mean?
Bloc.right: Neither group of allies can govern alone
wrong: A party has won a majority alone
No bloc, let alone a party, reached 61.
The president must rule the country instead of the parties
Bloc.exp: Unaligned parties or broken promises may decide the outcome.

Bloc.q: How is a bloc different from a coalition?
Bloc.right: A bloc usually works together; a coalition governs
wrong: A bloc is a single party, while a coalition is a party that wins alone
A bloc is a group of parties.
A bloc is the opposition only
Bloc.exp: A bloc is parties that usually cooperate; a coalition is the governing agreement.

Pro of coalitions.q: Which is a benefit of Israel's coalition system?
wrong: Only the largest party has a voice

Pro of coalitions.q: Why do small parties gain influence in coalitions?
wrong: Small parties automatically get to choose the prime minister in every election
Pro of coalitions.exp: Their seats can make or break a majority.

Con of coalitions.q: Which is a weakness of coalition governments?
Con of coalitions.right: They can collapse if partners leave
wrong: The Knesset cannot pass any laws at all
Con of coalitions.exp: Your quick check: true that a coalition can fall apart.

Con of coalitions.q: A partner leaves the coalition and it drops below 61. What may follow?
Con of coalitions.right: The government falls; new elections may follow
wrong: The president takes over the government and rules alone until the next year
Con of coalitions.exp: Coalitions are fragile; the government can fall.

Ruled-out partners.q: Your coalition of 73 seats needed Yashar, which promised not to sit with Netanyahu. What best describes this coalition?
Ruled-out partners.right: Possible on paper but hard to form
wrong: Certain to form because it has 73 seats
Seat math doesn't overcome a promise not to join.
Ruled-out partners.exp: "A coalition with 61 seats is mathematically possible, but that does not mean the parties would agree."

Ruled-out partners.q: How do ruled-out partners make forming a government harder?
wrong: They make it easier, since fewer parties need to agree on a shared plan
Ruled-out partners.exp: Promises not to sit with rivals limit the paths to 61.

Torah to tradition.q: Which example best fits the path from Torah to rabbinic interpretation to tradition?
Torah to tradition.right: Simchat Torah, a celebration not in the Torah
wrong: The Ten Commandments given at Sinai
Joseph rationing grain in Egypt during the famine
Torah to tradition.exp: Simchat Torah grew from the custom of finishing and restarting the Torah.

Torah to tradition.q: Which step comes right after the written Torah in your notes' path?
wrong: Jewish history, the last step, which comes once customs have spread widely
Torah to tradition.exp: Torah → rabbinic interpretation → tradition → Jewish history.

Simchat Torah.q: Why do Jews begin Bereishit right after finishing Devarim on Simchat Torah?
Simchat Torah.right: To show learning should never stop
wrong: Because the Torah commands that exact day
Simchat Torah is not in the Torah.
Because Devarim was too long to finish
Because Moshe asked to be read twice
Simchat Torah.exp: Your notes: 'We should never stop learning Torah.'

Simchat Torah.q: Simchat Torah is best used as evidence that
Simchat Torah.right: traditions can develop beyond the text
wrong: every Jewish holiday is commanded word for word in the written Torah
It's not commanded in the text.
Simchat Torah.exp: It isn't commanded in the text, yet it became a tradition.

Shmini Atzeret.q: According to your notes, how is the extra day after Sukkot explained?
Shmini Atzeret.right: The celebration was too good to end
wrong: It was added by Pharaoh in Egypt
It marks the creation of Adam and Eve
It does not replace Yom Kippur.
Shmini Atzeret.exp: "A party you don't want to end."

Shmini Atzeret.q: How do Israel and other places differ about Simchat Torah?
Shmini Atzeret.right: In Israel it falls on Shmini Atzeret
wrong: In Israel it is not celebrated at all, only in communities outside the land
It is; same day as Shmini Atzeret.
Shmini Atzeret.exp: In Israel Simchat Torah is the same day as Shmini Atzeret.

Oral and written Torah.q: How does the idea of oral tradition help explain new customs?
Oral and written Torah.right: Interpretation can grow around a fixed text
wrong: The written Torah keeps being rewritten
Your notes say it can't be changed.
Customs come only from written law
Many customs are not in the Torah.
Oral tradition replaced the written Torah long ago
Oral and written Torah.exp: The text stays; interpretation and custom grow.

Oral and written Torah.q: What does comparing the written Torah to a constitution suggest?
Oral and written Torah.right: It is fixed, so interpretation does the adapting
wrong: It can be rewritten each year by vote, like an ordinary law in a parliament
Oral and written Torah.exp: A fixed text, with oral tradition carrying interpretation.

Common core, local form.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the Rosh Hashanah traditions article?
Common core, local form.right: Communities kept a shared core but adapted it locally
wrong: Every community ate exactly the same foods
Customs never changed after the Torah
Many developed later, some in medieval times.
Local foods replaced the holiday's meaning in every community
The meaning stayed; the form changed.
Common core, local form.exp: Bene Israel and Cochin Jews each adapted to their region's ingredients.

Common core, local form.q: Which example best shows a common core with local form?
Common core, local form.right: Different foods for the same hope of a good year
wrong: All communities using exactly the same foods and blessings on Rosh Hashanah
Common core, local form.exp: Shared hope; local foods, words and customs.

Apples and honey.q: What does the dating of apples and honey to the 1300s show about traditions?
wrong: All customs come straight from Sinai
Apples and honey are commanded in the Torah

Apples and honey.q: What does the 1300s date for apples and honey suggest?
Apples and honey.right: Even familiar customs developed over time
wrong: The custom is written in the Torah and has existed since the time of Avraham
Apples and honey.exp: A medieval custom shows how traditions grow.

Beta Israel.q: What best explains why customs that seem universal were not central to Ethiopian Jews?
Beta Israel.right: They developed apart from other communities
wrong: They observed it as Brenha Serkan.
They had no access to any food
They had foods like injera and lamb.
They lived in medieval Germany near the city of Worms
Beta Israel.exp: Isolation meant a different path of development.

Beta Israel.q: Beta Israel's customs best support which conclusion?
Beta Israel.right: Isolation from rabbinic communities shaped practice
wrong: All Jewish communities practiced exactly the same customs in every age
Beta Israel invented apples and honey
Beta Israel.exp: Developing apart from rabbinic communities, they didn't center these customs.

Turkish Jews and honey.q: What does the Turkish sugar custom show about how traditions adapt?
Turkish Jews and honey.right: The meaning is kept while the form changes
wrong: The wish for sweetness was abandoned
Sugar keeps the wish for sweetness.
Honey was banned in the Torah
Every Jewish community copied it from Izmir
It was specific to some families.
Turkish Jews and honey.exp: Keep the sweetness, change the food.

Turkish Jews and honey.q: The Izmir sugar custom shows a tradition adapting while keeping
Turkish Jews and honey.right: the goal of a sweet year
wrong: the exact same food used in every other community during the holiday
Turkish Jews and honey.exp: Sugar replaced honey, but the hope for sweetness stayed.

Knowledge.q: "A Torah scroll is valuable, but someone must know how to read it." What larger point is the author making?
Knowledge.right: Objects need knowledge to keep meaning
wrong: Torah scrolls should be replaced by books
The point is about knowledge, not format.
Only teachers should own Torah scrolls
Physical objects matter more than people
Knowledge.exp: Education turns objects into a living tradition.

Knowledge.q: Why does a community need teachers to survive?
Knowledge.right: Texts and practices must be taught
wrong: Because buildings matter more than people, and teachers keep the buildings
Knowledge.exp: Texts, laws, prayers and practices must pass to the next generation.

Institutions.q: Why aren't texts and traditions alone enough to sustain a community?
wrong: Texts are always lost when people move
Traditions are not part of Jewish life
Communities need only food and shelter
That helps individuals, not a community.
Institutions.exp: Your answer named synagogues, schools, cemeteries and courts.

Institutions.q: Which is an example of an institution from your notes?
wrong: A single family praying at home without any connection to other families
Institutions.exp: Synagogue, school, cemetery, charity, court and care for the poor and sick.

Adaptation balance.q: A community changes everything to fit its new country. What problem does the reading warn about?
Adaptation balance.right: Nothing distinct may be left to preserve
wrong: It will survive more easily forever
The reading warns of losing what makes it distinct.
It will refuse to learn the language
It will have far too many institutions to support
Adaptation balance.exp: Your teacher asked: what happens when a community totally assimilates?

Adaptation balance.q: A community refuses to change anything after moving. What risk does it face?
wrong: It will lose everything distinctive about itself within a single generation
That's the risk of adapting completely.
Adaptation balance.exp: Refusing to adapt makes survival hard.

Portable civilization.q: Which statement best explains how Jewish communities survived many displacements?
Portable civilization.right: Their core could move with them
wrong: They never moved from one place
They gave up all their traditions
Portable civilization.exp: Texts, knowledge, rituals, institutions and memory can be rebuilt.

Portable civilization.q: Which feature most made Jewish civilization portable?
Portable civilization.right: Texts that travel and knowledge that can be retaught
wrong: Dependence on one building in one city that everyone had to visit often
It never depended on one building.
It didn't depend on one language.
It didn't depend on one country.
Portable civilization.exp: Texts travel; knowledge can be retaught; institutions rebuilt.
